newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia buys Cuban raw sugar cargoes for Q2 -trade.
newsitem.headline: Russia buys Cuban raw sugar cargoes for Q2 -trade.

text.p: Russia will take delivery of several cargoes of Cuban raw sugar during the next two months, Moscow-based sources at trading houses said on Tuesday.

The sources said that Russia had imported only small tonnages, if any, this year under a Cuba-Russia sugar-for-oil barter deal, and that Russian firms were taking up the slack by buying directly from international commodities houses.

"At least as far as our company is concerned, we expect a few shipments of Cuban sugar to Russia in the second quarter," said Vladimir Bjedougov, deputy director of the international department at Russian trader Alfa-Eko.
He could not specify tonnages but said a typical cargo should be 25,000 tonnes.

Several sugar traders in London and Moscow said that between 50,000 and 150,000 tonnes of raws, the bulk of which was likely to be Cuban, would be delivered to Russia soon. Some said the total could be even higher.
One Moscow-based trader said 50,000 tonnes was on its way to the Dobrinsky sugar refinery near Lipetsk, south of Moscow, via Riga.
Other traders said raw sugar may be coming through Riga because Russia's Black Sea port of Novorossiisk was badly congested.

Bjedounov said it was hard to estimate the amount of raw sugar imported into Russia so far this year because purchases by private commercial buyers outside the intergovernmental oil-for-sugar barter deal with Cuba were harder to track.

A communist-era protocol exchanging Russian oil for Cuban sugar was the backbone of trade between the two countries until recent years, when market reforms in Russia put the deals under increasing commercial pressure.
Traders said sugar deliveries under the 1996 protocol still had to be completed, and that a new barter deal for swaps this year had not yet been finalised.

Official statistics for January-February, the last months for which data were available, put Russian raw sugar imports at 66,100 tonnes from countries outside the Commonwealth of Independent States, a meagre 27 percent of year-ago levels.
Bjedounov said one reason for the slump was that Alfa-Eko and Russian trade house Menatep were importing substantial quantities of raw sugar in 1996 under official oil-for-sugar protocols.
"Last year the protocol (with Cuba) was implemented and our company and Menatep delivered substantial (early) volumes of Cuban raws into Russia," he said.
